$comment: Budgets for the weight of this service's production dependency tree, checked by `pnpm deps:weight`.
paul-explore gained a gzipped first-load-JS budget (gpbsumido/paul-explore#396). That metric is
meaningless here — this service ships no browser bundle, so the same check would produce a number
that can go red without anything being wrong, which is worse than no check at all.
What costs a user on this service is cold start. It scales to zero — fly.toml sets
`auto_stop_machines = "stop"` and `min_machines_running = 0` — so a full boot sits on the critical
path of someone's first request. The two things that drive that boot are how much has to be
installed and paged in, and how much work happens at import time. These budgets guard the first of
those.
Say the quiet part: dependency weight is a PROXY for cold start, not cold start. paul-explore's
budget measures the bytes a browser genuinely waits on; this one measures a correlate. It is gated
anyway because it is deterministic and the thing it correlates with is not — see 'what is not
budgeted' below.
How the numbers are taken: a `pnpm install --prod --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts` into a throwaway
directory, with supportedArchitectures pinned to linux/x64/glibc, then a walk of the resulting tree
deduplicating by inode so pnpm's hardlinks and symlinks are each counted once.
The architecture pin exists because sharp ships a different prebuilt libvips per platform, so an
unpinned run resolves whatever the host happens to be. It narrows that; it does not close it, and I
would rather write down what it actually does than what I first assumed it did. CI, on real linux,
reads 170,541,700 bytes across 332 packages. The same command on an arm64 Mac reads 190,888,101
across 334, because pnpm can only filter by libc when it is running on the libc in question — off
linux it keeps both the glibc and the musl sharp builds, and the extra pair is the 20 MiB gap.
One correction to 'byte-identical', which is true per host and not across hosts. I measured this in
a local linux/amd64 container before CI ran and got 170,541,682, eighteen bytes under the runner.
Both are stable on repeat. Eighteen bytes on 170 MB changes no decision, but the honest form of the
claim is that the figure is reproducible on a given machine, and CI's is the one that counts.
That gap is worth more attention now than it was at 4.11.3. It is the same 20,346,401 bytes it
always was, but the tree it sits in is 61% smaller, so it went from 4.6% of the total to 12%. The
local reading is still the higher one, so a laptop run that passes cannot be a CI run that fails,
and CI is still the authoritative figure because it is the platform that actually cold starts. What
changed is that the budget can no longer sit comfortably above both at the old proportions: 8% over
the local reading is now 21% over CI, where it used to be 13%. The local number binds, and the
budget below is set against it.
`--ignore-scripts` is a known understatement, and at 4.11.4 it finally became a true one. It always
said that ffmpeg-static downloads its binary in a postinstall hook and so the deployed image is
larger than the number here by roughly that binary. That was wrong in a way nobody checked: pnpm 10
does not run a dependency's build script unless the package is named in pnpm.onlyBuiltDependencies,
nothing was, and so the download had never run anywhere — not on a laptop, not in the Docker image.
The understatement was zero because the binary was simply absent, and the video path was broken.
That is fixed, which means the gap is now real and about 80 MB on linux/x64. Still excluded, for the
original reason: the download is not pinned by the lockfile and not reproducible offline, so
including it would trade a deterministic gate for a flaky one. This measures what the lockfile can
account for, and that boundary is now written down accurately rather than aspirationally.
What is not budgeted, and why:
- Boot wall-clock. Importing the built app takes 268-294 ms on an idle laptop; on a shared CI runner
that spread is far wider. Gating on it would produce failures that re-run green, and a guard that
flakes gets ignored or deleted. Measure it by hand when it matters.
- Bundle size. There is no bundle. See above.
- The boot path itself. mediaProcessor is imported eagerly from src/index.ts, so sharp and ffmpeg
load on every boot including requests that never touch media. That is a real cold-start cost these
budgets cannot see, because it is about when a module loads rather than how much was installed.
Raising a budget is a fine thing to do when the weight bought something. Do it in the same commit as
the dependency, so the diff shows the trade rather than just the fix.

installBytes.why: Total bytes of a production-only install, the proxy for install time and image size on a scale-to-zero boot. At 4.11.4 CI measures 170,541,700 (162.64 MiB) and an arm64 Mac measures 190,888,101 (182.05 MiB), each stable across repeated runs on that host. This leaves about 23% headroom against CI and about 10% against the higher local reading, which is the one that binds. Down from 500,000,000 at 4.11.3, when the tree was 443,101,142 on CI: replacing ffprobe-static with @ffprobe-installer/ffprobe took 272,559,442 bytes out on both platforms, because the old package shipped a prebuilt ffprobe for six platforms in one tarball and this service runs one of them. Leaving the budget at its old ceiling after a win that size would have left a number that could not fail.

packageCount.why: Number of resolved production packages including transitives, the proxy for module-resolution work at import time. At 4.11.4 CI measures 332 and an arm64 Mac measures 334, the two extra being the musl sharp builds a non-linux host cannot filter out. About 8% headroom against CI. Deliberately NOT lowered at 4.11.4, because this is the one number the ffprobe work pushed the wrong way: one fat package became a wrapper plus one platform package, so the count went up by one while the bytes fell by 260 MiB. That is the trade working as intended, and it is why two proxies are gated rather than one. Counted as entries in the virtual store, so a package resolved twice at different versions counts twice — which is right, because Node pays for both.
